title: bug: rollback's dump walk cannot see a deployment.migrate_down, so a revert after the target makes a restoring rollback apply the wrong schema
description:
Parent: task-705977238f794b2cadb5c1dcdb98d6bd (found during its QA rework; same data-loss class, out of that row's one-rule scope). selectRollbackDumpDecision (apps/daemon/src/deployment/rollback-preflight.ts) walks readDeployLedger ONLY, but deployment.migrate_down (migrate-down-command.ts -> revertLastBatch, migration-down-service.ts:144) records a REVERTED migration receipt under its OWN requestId and writes no deploy receipt, so the walk never sees that schema move.
Shape, by code read (NOT executed - re-measure first): A -> B (migrates) -> migrate_down (reverts B's batch, schema back to A's) -> D (migrates; D.backupRef = schema A) -> rollback to B WITH restore: the walk skips nothing, stops at D, applies D's dump and starts B's image on schema A with no refusal.
Fix direction for the architect: the walk needs the environment's schema moves in order (deploy migrations, migrate_down reverts, restoring rollbacks), or must refuse when a revert it cannot order sits after the target.
definitionOfDone: A test drives A -> B(migrates) -> deployment.migrate_down -> D(migrates) through production writers/handlers, then a rollback to B WITH restore, and asserts it either refuses with a stable code AND layer or applies the migrate_down's own pre-revert dump - never D's dump - with the restore port's recorded calls read back.
The new arm is proven non-vacuous by a mutation drill that removes the new rule and reds it.
`pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` EXIT 0 with the `Test Files N passed (N)` count line quoted.

implementationPlan.description:
BUILD THE ORDERED SCHEMA-MOVE VIEW, in its own small module.

Enumerate migration receipts with store.enumerateAggregateIdsByPrefix over the 'migration:' prefix - the same payload-free indexed range scan policy-risk-reader.ts and policy-waiver-reader.ts already use. Read each receipt, keep only this projectId and this environment, and keep only outcomes that actually MOVED the schema: APPLIED and REVERTED. Exclude REFUSED - it leaves the schema untouched, and including it would invent moves that never happened.

ORDER BY decidedAt, NOT BY THE SCAN. The prefix scan returns ids sorted by id and the id is a SHA256, so scan order carries no chronology. Note the cost in the step note: this reads every migration receipt payload for the project. That is acceptable because rollback is rare; do not put it on a hot read and do not cache it across commands.

Be precise about what each dump represents. A REVERTED receipt's backupRef is the state before THE REVERT, not before the original migration. Getting this backwards restores the wrong schema while looking correct.

Create the .ts and its .js bridge together, the way the neighbouring deployment modules have theirs.

ORDER IS `decision_position` AND THE MODULE NEVER SORTS. It walks store.readCommandDecisionsAfter from 0n in pages of 200, the same paged walk readDeployLedger uses, and appends in arrival order. decidedAt is never read at all - not to order, not to filter. That is stronger than sorting by position: there is no key to get wrong.

  - migration receipt (principal + kind + projectId) that will not decode: MIGRATION_UNVERIFIED. Undecodable bytes carry no environment, so it cannot be shown to belong elsewhere and refuses in every environment of the project. Fail closed.
  - decodes, then re-read through `readMigrationReceipt` (the production reader) so kind/disposition/aggregate-id/receipt-id rules live in ONE place: throws -> MIGRATION_UNVERIFIED; null -> skipped; other environment -> skipped.

  - backupRef null: BACKUP_ABSENT. **THIS IS A DELIBERATE, DISCLOSED DEVIATION FROM STEP 3's AMENDED TEXT** - see below.

Skip", and separately says APPLIED-or-REVERTED-with-null-backupRef is the case that refuses. Cost, disclosed rather than hidden: a migration that refused before taking its dump left the schema standing, so this is a FALSE refusal for a rollback a later deploy's dump could have served. It costs a refusal; the other direction costs a database. Recorded in the module's own comment at the branch, in a row comment, and raised with the architect in chat.

TARGET POSITION - HOW, WITHOUT DUPLICATING readDeployLedger. deploy-ledger.ts:242 keys every deploy receipt decision `{commandId: receiptId, principalId: DEPLOY_ENGINE_PRINCIPAL_ID, projectId}`, and getCommandDecision returns `decisionPosition`. So the caller reads the ALREADY-ADMITTED target's position with one keyed lookup and this module never re-derives the deploy filter. That was the alternative I rejected: re-implementing readDeployLedger's decode/aggregate-id/dedupe chain here would have been a second, drifting copy of the authority.

MARKER ENVIRONMENT. A marker's key carries none, so the caller injects `scope.environmentOfRollback(commandId)` built from readDeployLedger - the authority on which environment a receipt belongs to. null (a rollback that restored and then died before its receipt landed) is treated as a move in THIS environment, per the amendment: reading an applied restore as nothing-happened is the direction that pairs an old image with a newer schema.

amendments.description:
BUILD THE ORDERED SCHEMA-HISTORY VIEW, in its own small module (apps/daemon/src/deployment/rollback-schema-moves.ts plus its one-line .js bridge `export * from "./rollback-schema-moves.ts";`, created together). This text SUPERSEDES the base description. Two of its instructions were wrong and are reversed below.

THE MODEL. The walk is looking for the first DUMP taken after the target, with no dump-less schema move before it. A dump is a snapshot of the schema at the moment it was taken, whatever happened afterwards, so what matters about each record is (1) did it take a dump, and (2) could it have moved the schema without one.

ORDER BY LEDGER POSITION, NEVER BY decidedAt. REVERSED from the base text. Walk store.readCommandDecisionsAfter from cursor 0n, the same paged walk deploy-ledger.ts's readDeployLedger uses. Its cursor is the stored `decision_position` (packages/store/src/decision-read-model.ts), a monotonic commit order. decidedAt is a wall clock: every rollback fixture in this directory uses a constant clock (rollback-command-ordering.test.ts `clock = () => "2026-09-06T01:00:00.000Z"`), so sorting by it ties on every record and falls back to SHA order. Production can also tie within a millisecond or step backwards across a clock adjustment. One walk of the ledger gives the target deploy receipt, every migration receipt and every restore marker in one total order, which also removes the need for the prefix scan.

CLASSIFY EACH RECORD after the target, for this projectId and environment only:
  - migration receipt with non-null backupRef, ANY outcome including REFUSED: a SNAPSHOT. REVERSED from the base text, which excluded REFUSED. migration-down-service.ts takes its dump BEFORE it reverts and returns `{ ...refused(base, code, code), backupRef }` on failure, including the path where the revert COMMITTED and the post-revert name check then threw. That dump is still the schema at the moment it was taken. Excluding it walks on to a later dump, which is the data-loss direction.
  - migration receipt APPLIED or REVERTED with null backupRef: a DUMP-LESS MOVE. Refuse, never skip.
  - migration receipt REFUSED with null backupRef: refused before any dump, schema untouched. Skip.
  - restore marker (principal ROLLBACK_RESTORE_PRINCIPAL): a DUMP-LESS MOVE. Refuse. A marker carries no environment in its key; resolve it through the rollback's own records for the same commandId, and if the environment cannot be established, treat the marker as a move in THIS environment, because reading an applied restore as nothing-happened is the unsafe direction.
  - deploy receipts: position only, needed to locate the target.

A REVERTED receipt's backupRef is the state before THE REVERT, not before the original migration. That is exactly the schema a rollback to the deploy before the revert wants.

Note the cost in the step note: one full ledger walk per restoring rollback. Acceptable because rollback is rare. Do not put it on a hot read and do not cache it across commands.
amendments.reason: Two defects in the base text, both measured. First, ordering by decidedAt ties: every rollback fixture uses a constant clock, so the step-2 arm would pass or fail on SHA order. The ledger has a true commit-order key, decision_position, behind store.readCommandDecisionsAfter. Second, excluding every REFUSED receipt discards real dumps: migration-down-service.ts takes its dump BEFORE reverting and keeps backupRef on a refusal, including the case where the revert committed but the post-check threw. Skipping that receipt walks on to a LATER dump.

implementationPlan.description:
WIRE THE WALK TO THE ORDERED VIEW, and preserve the parent's rules.

selectRollbackDumpDecision stops iterating deploy receipts and instead walks the environment's schema moves in order, forward from the target, taking the first move after it. A revert is now visible, so the scenario in step 2 resolves correctly.

THE DoD ALLOWS EITHER ANSWER: apply the migrate_down's own pre-revert dump, or refuse with a stable code AND layer. Choose deliberately and say why in the step note. Refusing is the safe fallback for a move the view genuinely cannot place; it should not be the answer for one it CAN place, because that would make restoring rollback unusable on any environment that has ever run a migrate_down.

  - a null backupRef refuses DEPLOY_ROLLBACK_RESTORE_BACKUP_ABSENT rather than skipping to a later dump, because a later dump is a later state and would destroy more than the rollback asked for;
  - a receipt that will not decode answers DEPLOY_ROLLBACK_RESTORE_MIGRATION_UNVERIFIED.
Add arms pinning both if the parent did not already, so this row cannot silently drop them.

The step 2 arm should now be green.

WIRED. `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon typecheck` EXIT 0; `vitest run src/deployment` = Test Files 26 passed (26), Tests 356 passed | 2 skipped (358). Step-2's arm (x) is GREEN. rollback-preflight.ts 245 lines, rollback-schema-moves.ts 208 - both under the 250 target.

THE LOOP NOW: readDeployLedger for the target and for placing markers; readEnvironmentSchemaMoves for the history; then one pass taking the FIRST move past the anchor. SNAPSHOT -> `{dumpDecisionId: move.requestId, ok:true}`. Any other verdict is returned VERBATIM as the refusal code, so the view and the walk cannot disagree about what a record means. Walk runs out -> MIGRATION_UNKNOWN, unchanged. `restoredBy` is gone; markers are in the view.

I CHOSE THE DUMP, NOT A REFUSAL, for the migrate_down - the answer amend-2 names. The revert's own pre-revert dump is the first snapshot after B and it holds B's schema, which arm (x) asserts by CONTENT ("-- a_table,b_table\n"), not only by filename.

THE ONE DESIGN DECISION THE PLAN DID NOT NAME, AND IT IS LOAD-BEARING: THE ANCHOR.
Measured, not assumed - deploy-service.ts:310 `const migrated = await migrateFor(...)` runs BEFORE `record(request, target, digest, null, releaseDecision)` at :335. So in PRODUCTION a deploy's migration receipt commits BEFORE its own deploy receipt. Anchoring the walk on the target's DEPLOY RECEIPT position would therefore put the target's own migration BEFORE the anchor in production but AFTER it in any history assembled receipt-first - and rollback-command-ordering.test.ts's historyHarness is assembled receipt-first (`h.deploy(...)` then `await h.migrate(...)`). I checked what that costs: under a receipt anchor, arm (vii) selects dep-b's OWN dump instead of refusing SCHEMA_OVERWRITTEN, because b's migration lands after b's receipt there. Same code, different answer by write order.
So `anchorPosition` uses THE TARGET'S OWN MIGRATION RECEIPT when it has one, and only falls back to its deploy receipt otherwise. That is also the semantically right anchor: the schema the target ran against is established by the target's own migration, not by the receipt that reports the deployment afterwards. It makes the walk order-independent, and (vii)/(viii)/(ix) stay green untouched.
The deploy-receipt fallback is ONE keyed read - deploy-ledger.ts:242 keys every receipt decision `{commandId: receiptId, principalId: DEPLOY_ENGINE_PRINCIPAL_ID, projectId}` - so readDeployLedger's filter is never duplicated.

THE THREE RULES, EACH PINNED BY AN ARM THAT REDS IF THE RULE GOES:

  2 MIGRATION_UNVERIFIED - NEW arm (xiii). Nothing pinned this behaviourally before; rollback-restore.test.ts:522 only listed the code in the DETAILS roster. Corruption cannot come from recordMigrationReceipt, so the arm commits the decision directly under the key+kind the reader recognises, asserts EFFECTS_COMMITTED so a refused write cannot make it vacuous, and again puts a readable dump after it.
  3 SCHEMA_OVERWRITTEN - parent's rollback-command-ordering.test.ts (vii), STILL GREEN after the rewrite, quoted here: `it("(vii) a RESTORING rollback between the target and its first migration refuses, restoring nothing")` asserting `{code:"DEPLOY_ROLLBACK_RESTORE_SCHEMA_OVERWRITTEN", layer: ROLLBACK_RESTORE_STAMP, detail: ROLLBACK_RESTORE_DETAILS.DEPLOY_ROLLBACK_RESTORE_SCHEMA_OVERWRITTEN}`.
NOT OVER-APPLIED: (viii) restoreDatabase:false is still skipped and dep-d's dump still wins; (ix) a migration before a restoring rollback still wins. Both green.

TWO ORDERING ARMS, and (xi) IS WHAT MAKES THE ORDERING KEY LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN TIDINESS:
